blocks.text: Binary search on answer generalizes binary search far beyond searching a sorted array. The key insight: binary search only requires that a PREDICATE function of your candidate answer is monotonic, meaning once it becomes true it stays true (or once false, stays false) as the candidate moves in one direction. You do not need a literal sorted array at all, you need a sorted TRUTH VALUE across the space of possible answers.
This reframing unlocks binary search for an entire category of optimization problems that do not look, on the surface, like searching problems at all.

Recognize the pattern: the question asks for a minimum or maximum value satisfying some condition, and VERIFYING whether one specific candidate value works is easier than directly computing the optimal value. This "guess and check, then binary search the guesses" framing is the giveaway.

blocks.caption: The feasibility predicate is false for small candidates and true for large candidates, with a single boundary point, exactly the shape binary search requires.

blocks.text: Define the search range [lo, hi] over the space of POSSIBLE ANSWERS, not array indices. Define a boolean feasible(x) predicate that answers "does candidate x satisfy the requirement." Binary search this range, calling feasible(mid) at each step and shrinking the range based on the monotonic property, exactly like standard binary search shrinks based on a comparison against a target value.

Given piles of bananas and h hours, find the minimum eating speed k (bananas per hour) such that Koko can finish all piles within h hours, where each pile takes ceil(pile / k) hours to finish at speed k, and a new pile cannot be started in the same hour an old one finished.

The candidate answer is the eating speed k. The predicate feasible(k) asks "can Koko finish everything within h hours at speed k." This predicate is monotonic: if speed k works, any FASTER speed also works, since eating faster can only reduce or keep equal the total hours needed. That monotonic property is exactly what makes binary search valid here.

blocks.caption: Standard binary search shrinking: when feasible(mid) is true, the answer might be smaller so hi shrinks to mid; when false, the answer must be larger so lo moves past mid.

blocks.text: Tracing piles = [3, 6, 7, 11], h = 8: at speed 4, hours needed = ceil(3/4) + ceil(6/4) + ceil(7/4) + ceil(11/4) = 1+2+2+3 = 8, exactly fits, feasible. At speed 3, hours = 1+2+3+4 = 10, exceeds 8, not feasible. Binary search between lo=1 and hi=11 (max pile) converges on the minimum feasible speed, which is 4.

The same template generalizes directly. In "Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days," the candidate answer is a ship capacity, and feasible(capacity) asks whether all packages can be shipped within D days at that capacity, greedily loading each day until the next package would exceed capacity. Larger capacity always ships in fewer or equal days, so the predicate is monotonic and the same binary search shrinks toward the minimum feasible capacity.

In "Split Array Largest Sum," the candidate answer is the maximum allowed subarray sum, and feasible(maxSum) asks whether the array can be split into at most m subarrays where every subarray sums to at most maxSum. Again, a larger maxSum only ever needs fewer or equal subarrays, giving the same monotonic shape.

The overall complexity is O(log(range) times cost of feasible)), where range is the size of the candidate answer space (hi minus lo initially) and the feasible check itself typically costs O(n) to scan the input once. These two factors multiply because the O(n) feasible check runs once per binary search iteration, and there are O(log(range)) iterations total.

For Koko Eating Bananas specifically, range is bounded by the largest pile size, so the total complexity is O(n log(maxPile)), a substantial improvement over any approach that tries every candidate speed one at a time, which would cost O(n times maxPile) in the worst case.

Picking correct initial values for lo and hi matters as much as the shrinking logic itself. lo should be the smallest value that could possibly be feasible (in Koko's case, speed 1, since speed 0 cannot make progress), and hi should be a value that is GUARANTEED feasible so the search always has a valid answer to converge toward (the largest single pile, since eating at that speed finishes every pile in one hour each).

Choosing hi too small (a value that is not actually always feasible) is a subtle bug: the binary search will still run and terminate without any error, but it can converge on a value that looks like an answer without actually being the true minimum, since the search never considered larger values that might have been necessary.

Forgetting to verify the predicate is actually monotonic before applying this technique: if it is not monotonic, binary search silently converges on a wrong answer with no runtime error at all, since the shrinking logic assumes a single boundary point that may not exist.

Off by one errors in the loop termination: searching for the minimum true value uses hi = mid (keep mid, since it might still be the answer) and lo = mid + 1 (definitely rule out mid). Searching for a MAXIMUM true value flips this: typically lo = mid and hi = mid minus 1, paired with computing mid using a rounded up midpoint to avoid an infinite loop when lo and hi are adjacent.

items: Koko Eating Bananas: minimum feasible eating speed.
Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days: minimum feasible ship capacity.
Split Array Largest Sum: minimum feasible maximum subarray sum.
Minimum Number of Days to Make m Bouquets: minimum feasible number of days, with an extra twist where feasible() itself requires a linear scan checking for m groups of k consecutive bloomed flowers.
Can you recognize the "minimum or maximum value satisfying a condition, checking one candidate is easy" signal that suggests this technique?
Can you write the feasible() predicate and argue out loud why it is monotonic before writing any binary search code?
Can you correctly write the shrinking logic for finding a MINIMUM feasible value versus a MAXIMUM feasible value without mixing up the two termination patterns?
Can you state the combined time complexity as the product of the search range's log and the feasibility check's cost?

description: Learn to binary search over a space of candidate answers using a monotonic feasibility predicate instead of searching a literal sorted array
